ad7_k12.topic: K-12 funding by local property tax: Rodriguez, funding gaps, counter-evidence

claims.text: Rodriguez decided 21 March 1973 (argued 12 October 1972), 5-4; majority by Justice Powell joined by Burger, Stewart, Blackmun, Rehnquist; dissents by Brennan, White (joined by Douglas, Brennan) and Marshall (joined by Douglas); education not a fundamental right; Texas did not create a suspect class based on poverty; financing need only be rationally related to a legitimate state interest

Edgewood (about 22,000 students) raised about $26 per pupil from property taxes despite the area's highest tax rate; Alamo Heights (about 5,000 students) raised $333 at a lower rate; with state and federal money Edgewood spent $356 and Alamo Heights $594 per pupil

Powell: education 'is not among the rights afforded explicit protection' by the Constitution; left open a claim if a system caused an 'absolute denial of educational opportunities'; Marshall called the holding 'a retreat from our historic commitment to equality of educational opportunity'; Texas Supreme Court 1989 required 'a substantially equal opportunity' to access funds; 2020 Sixth Circuit panel ruling vacated after Michigan settled

Texas courts ruled the Texas system unconstitutional in 1991, 1992 and 2005 and constitutional in 1995 and 2016; most states have faced school-funding litigation; Education Law Center (2021): 14 states spend more per pupil in low-poverty districts; Nevada $12,798 vs $8,731

EdBuild (Feb 2019): predominantly white districts receive $23bn more than districts serving mostly students of color; $2,226 less per student in the average nonwhite district; high-poverty nonwhite districts about $1,600 below national average vs about $130 for high-poverty white districts; mostly white districts average just over 1,500 students vs over 10,000 for nonwhite; cost-of-living adjusted

Ed Trust Funding Gaps 2018: highest-poverty districts get about $1,000 (7%) less per pupil in state and local funding than lowest-poverty; $2,000 (16%) after adjusting for the added cost of educating low-income students; districts serving the most students of color about $1,800 (13%) less; federal funds excluded

Chingos (Urban, 2013-14 data): districts attended by poor students received $12,961 per student vs $12,640 for non-poor (2.5% more, all sources); local funding about 15% lower for poor students (gap 18% in 1994-95, 14% in 2013-14); state funding about 10 points higher for poor students; EdBuild: 35 states allocate extra money for low-income students
Urban Institute revised its national study (2022) to fix charter-school accounting; Pennsylvania moved from poor students getting 4% more to 3% less

Jackson, Johnson, Persico: 10% increase in per-pupil spending each year for all twelve years leads to 0.27 more years of education, 7.25% higher wages and a 3.67-point reduction in annual adult poverty; effects much more pronounced for children from low-income families

ad7_debtlaw.topic: Student debt: totals, default and collections status 2026, bankruptcy law history 1976-2005, 2022 DOJ process, lobbying record

claims.text: Before 1976 educational debt was dischargeable in bankruptcy; the Commission on the Bankruptcy Laws (created 1970, P.L. 91-354) recommended in 1973 that governmental loans be nondischargeable for five years after repayment began, except for undue hardship; Education Amendments of 1976, P.L. 94-482 s.127(a), added HEA s.439A; effective date delayed nearly a year partly to await a GAO study (GAO-HRD-77-83, April 1977)

Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1978, P.L. 95-598 s.316, repealed s.439A; the House Judiciary bill H.R. 8200 would have restored dischargeability but a floor amendment restored nondischargeability by voice vote, now 11 U.S.C. 523(a)(8); the House Report stated that 'less than 1% of all federally insured and guaranteed educational loans were discharged in bankruptcy'

1990 Crime Control Act P.L. 101-647 s.3621 lengthened the five-year period to seven; the 1997 National Bankruptcy Review Commission recommended eliminating 523(a)(8); Higher Education Amendments of 1998 P.L. 105-244 s.971 removed the time route; BAPCPA 2005 P.L. 109-8 s.220 extended nondischargeability to private educational loans; undue hardship undefined in the statute; courts generally apply Brunner (2d Cir. 1987)

P.L. 96-56 (approved 14 August 1979) widened 523(a)(8) to loans 'made, insured, or guaranteed by a governmental unit, or made under any program funded in whole or in part by a governmental unit or a nonprofit institution of higher education' and excluded suspension periods from the five years

1978 code covered debts owed to governmental units or nonprofit institutions of higher education and allowed a Chapter 13 superdischarge; 1984 legislation removed 'of higher education'; 1990 Congress extended five years to seven and removed student loans from the Chapter 13 superdischarge; 1991 Higher Education Technical Amendments eliminated the six-year statute of limitations on collecting defaulted student loans

Brunner test: (1) cannot maintain a minimal standard of living if forced to repay; (2) circumstances likely to persist for a significant part of the repayment period; (3) good-faith efforts to repay; conjunctive; about 70% of courts use Brunner and 16% a totality test (Pardo and Lacey 2005); 1973 HEW urged Congress after reports of student 'deadbeats'
DOJ/ED new process announced 17 November 2022: borrower attestation form plus Education Department data; DOJ applies undue-hardship factors and decides whether to recommend discharge; judge decides

DOJ (17 July 2024): 1,220 cases filed November 2022 to March 2024; 588 from October 2023 to March 2024 (+36%); 96% of borrowers used the attestation process; 98% of cases decided by courts gave full or partial discharge
DOJ issued a revised attestation form in May 2025; core framework unchanged as of September 2026

Stephen Burd (NPR, 2007): Sallie Mae spent $9 million lobbying Congress between 1999 and 2005, the years the bankruptcy bill was under consideration; its PAC gave more than $130,000 to members of the Judiciary Committees; no hearings were held on the private-loan provision

New America (29 May 2007): on who pushed the 2005 private-loan change, 'No one seems to know'; nothing in the Congressional Record explains it; Sallie Mae's internal strategy document listed preserving the provision's benefits as its number two item; lenders 'go to the front of the line' in bankruptcy
ED paused involuntary collections (wage garnishment, Treasury offset) on 16 January 2026 after sending warning notices in early January, citing OBBBA implementation; pause continued as of June 2026

As of 19 October 2026, ED and Treasury planned to resume administrative wage garnishment in fall 2026 with no date announced; garnishment can take up to 15% of disposable pay without a court order; about 7.7m in default at the start of 2026

9 December 2025: ED announced a proposed settlement with Missouri and other states to end SAVE: no new enrollments, pending applications denied, about 7 million enrollees moved to other plans; interest accruing since August 2025

NY Fed Q2 2026: student loan balances $1.65tn, down $7bn in the quarter and up $13bn on the year; flow into serious delinquency 7.83% (12.88% a year earlier), distorted by re-reporting of defaulted debt

FSA data to 30 June 2026: defaults up about 1.6m borrowers and $54bn in the first half of 2026; 31+-day delinquency 15.7% of dollars (18.6% Dec 2025); about 1.5m in late-stage delinquency; RAP enrollment not yet reported
Brookings (2015): federal student debt nearly quadrupled 2000-2014 to over $1.1tn; borrowers more than doubled to 42 million
